newsitem.title: CANADA: Hizbollah has network in Canada - report.
newsitem.headline: Hizbollah has network in Canada - report.

text.p: The fundamentalist group Hizbollah has a network in Canada designed to help members who want a safe haven in North America, a newspaper said on Saturday, quoting a Canadian spy agency document.

The document was filed with the Federal Court of Canada by the Canadian Security Intelligence Service to summarize evidence in a deportation case involving Saudi dissident Hani Abdel-Rahim al-Sayegh, the Globe and Mail reported.

CSIS alleged that Sayegh was involved in a bombing in Saudi Arabia last June that killed 19 U.S. airmen and wounded nearly 400 people. The agency said Sayegh conducted surveillance at the bomb site and drove a car that "signaled the explosives-laden truck to enter the parking lot."
Sayegh was arrested in Ottawa on March 18 on the grounds that he represented a security threat to Canada.

According to CSIS, the bombing was the work of a militant Shiite Moslem fundamentalist group with ties to Hizbollah -- a group called the Saudi Hizbollah. CSIS has said the Saudis found a detonator at the site of the bombing similar to a kind used in the past by the Lebanese Hizbollah.
Sayegh is allegedly a member of the Saudi Hizbollah, whose terrorist actions are supported and assisted by the Lebanese-based Hizbollah group, the newspaper quoted the CSIS document as saying.
Hizbollah's stated objectives include the establishment of a Shiite Islamic state in Lebanon, the removal of non-Islamic influences from the area and the elimination of Israel.
The leader of the Saudi Hizbollah radical Shiite movement is Sheikh Jaafar Mubarak, now under arrest in Saudi Arabia, the newspaper said.

The CSIS document is quoted as saying Hizbollah members have established "an infrastructure" in Canada and "receive and comply with direction from the Hizbollah leadership hierarchy in Lebanon." CSIS also cited the 1994 federal court case of Mohammed Hussein al-Husseini, another alleged Hizbollah terrorist living in Canada, the newspaper said.
"Al-Husseini ultimately admitted to being a member of Hizbollah," it quoted the summary as saying. "He further admitted that the terrorist group operates in Canada."

The man CSIS alleged masterminded the attack, Ahmed Ibrahim Ahmad Mughassil, is currently living in Iran under the protection of the government, according to a report in New York's Newsday newspaper on Saturday, citing unidentified sources.

The Saudi blast took place on June 25 at the Khobar Towers, a complex housing U.S. military personnel outside Dhahran in the oil-rich eastern part of the country. Sayegh has told reporters he was in Syria at the time.
He arrived in Canada requesting refugee status from Saudi Arabia because of the way the Sunni Moslem rulers treat Shiites.
